question: What is the meaning of modular design in relation to modularity and repairability?
description: Modular design, in relation to modularity and repairability, refers to the approach of breaking down a system or product into separate modules or components that can be easily replaced or repaired independently. This design strategy allows for efficient maintenance and repair by enabling the replacement of specific modules without affecting the functionality of the entire system.

5. Discussion 
The primary objective of this research was to develop DPPs using a 
modular ontology approach. To address this objective, a literature re­
view and interviews were conducted to gather the information re­
quirements that constitutes DPPs. Based on the literature review and 
interview findings, the research has identified the necessary IRs. Due to 
the wide coverage of various product lifecycle stages, diverse material 
compositions, and multi-faceted environmental impact considerations, 
DPPs tend to encompass a complex set of information, which compli­
cates their implementation (King et al., 2023; Plociennik et al., 2022). 
To address this challenge, the present study employed a modular 
ontology modeling approach to emphasize modularity, reusability, and 
interoperability in the ontology development for the DPP (Shimizu et al., 
2023). The key notions of DPPs identified from the literature and in­
dustry representatives are presented in the form of modules using an 
established ODPs. The use of ODPs provides a scalable structure that can 
handle the diverse and expansive requirements of DPPs. The modular 
design inherently supports reusability, allowing modules created for 
specific tasks or domains to be reused in different contexts with minimal 
modifications. This goes hand in hand with the core value of ontologies, 
which lies in their inherent capacity for reuse and interoperability 
(Hitzler, 2021). Furthermore, the ontology captures the semantics of the 
identified IRs, drawing on the ongoing standardization efforts by ISO, 
specifically ISO/DIS 59004. This standard focuses on circular economy 
terminology, principles, and guidance for implementation. We have 
used this standard to define the classes and properties in our ontology, 
demonstrating the adoption of standardized terminologies and defini­
tions across modules. Additionally, the key concepts are aligned with 
existing core ontologies, including BOT, BPO, Brick, REC, MAT and 
ENVO, to promote semantic interoperability and standardization of the 
key concepts. 
While ontologies are widely used for various purposes, most of them 
are not reused beyond their original use-cases (Shimizu et al., 2023). 
Reusing ontologies is difficult, for several reasons, such as differing 
representational granularity, and lack of conceptual clarity in design 
(Shimizu et al., 2023). This resonates with the challenges of imple­
menting DPPs, especially the integration of diverse data stemming from 
different sources. In this study, we address this challenge by segmenting 
domain-specific knowledge into separate modules, which promotes 
achieving better data integration particularly when dealing with het­
erogeneous sources. DPPs are live documents, or they are dynamic 
where the data landscape is continually evolving and requires consistent 
maintenance (G¨otz et al., 2022). This modular ontology design approach 
for implementing DPPs facilitates easier updates, enabling a more agile 
response to changes that may occur in the types of data gathered 
throughout the life cycle of a product. New modules can be added or 
existing ones could be easily extended, without triggering a chain of 
changes throughout the ontology. This shows that our modular ontology 
demonstrates a high degree of scalability, which is beneficial for future- 
proofing the ontology against emerging requirements. 
This research offers an important contribution to the domain of 
material and product passports, complementing the efforts of works like 
those by Kedir et al. (2021) and Sauter et al. (2019) in the construction 
industry. Our approach contributes uniquely by introducing a modular 
design that enhances interoperability and reusability across diverse 
domains. Furthermore, our work leverages standard and reusable 
ontology patterns to address challenges such as representational gran­
ularity. The contribution of this research, in relation to the scope and 
objectives of existing work, focuses on addressing the limitations of 
traditional ontology development for the circular economy. The existing 
ontologies for the circular economy, reviewed during the writing pro­
cess of this study, typically adopt a monolithic approach, which confines 
their reusability to their initial design. This problem is also discussed in 
the works of Li et al. (2023) and Blomqvist et al. (2023).

ontologies. It enhances semantic interoperability and flexibility across 
various domains and industry sectors. 
The practical implication of this research is considered from different 
aspects including the construction industry, consumers, policy makers, 
environmental, and social impact. For the construction industry, the use 
of such DPPs could make supply chain management more efficient by 
providing real-time, accurate data about products at every stage of their 
life cycle. For example, in our DPP ontology, this aspect is achieved by 
modeling the product's location and its movement through space and 
time, enabling tracking within the supply chain information. For con­
sumers, DPPs offer detailed information about product's origin, mate­
rials and environmental impact, enabling more informed purchasing 
decisions. This aspect of our DPP is modeled by making the ‘Product’ 
module as a specialization of the “EntityWithProvenance” pattern. For 
policy makers, the structured data modeling approach employed in the 
modular ontology could be used to inform more effective and targeted 
policy making and pave the way for improved interoperability between 
businesses and regulatory systems, making compliance easier and more 
effective. This aspect is shown in our DPP by modeling the regulatory 
requirements for products in the ‘Standard’ and ‘Certification’ modules, 
which provides a framework for compliance and quality assurance. 
Finally, the environmental and societal impacts of this research lie in the 
fact that the data provided by such DPPs could empower society to make 
sustainable choices and engage in the practice of sustainable consump­
tion. This encourages businesses and manufacturers to adopt sustainable 
production and manufacturing processes, which are modeled in our 
ontology using the ‘Manufacturer’ module. 
In developing a modular ontology for digital product passports using 
ODPs, we encountered some limitations. These include the limited 
coverage of existing ODPs and the absence of core modules specialized 
for unique modeling needs for the domain of circular economy. Addi­
tionally, there is a risk of ODP misuse, which can lead to the creation of 
unnecessarily complex, difficult-to-maintain, or semantically flawed 
ontologies. The complexity involved in selecting and applying the most 
appropriate ODP for specific modeling use cases poses a challenge. This 
can result in semantic inaccuracies if patterns are incorrectly applied. 
6. Conclusions 
The presented study explores the development of modular DPP on­
tologies aimed at advancing circular economy principles within the built 
environment. This undertaking is both timely and critical, considering 
the pressing need to shift from linear to circular models, particularly in 
sectors with significant environmental footprints like construction and 
infrastructure development. By facilitating the transparent documenta­
tion and tracking of materials and products throughout their lifecycle, 
our work on developing DPPs to promote the circular economy directly 
supports Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 12, which calls for sus­
tainable consumption and production patterns. DPPs can provide 
detailed information about the materials and processes involved in the 
production of building materials and products. This promotes trans­
parency in the supply chain enabling consumers and businesses to make 
more informed decisions based on sustainability criteria. This aligns 
with SDG 12’s emphasis on sustainable consumption patterns. By inte­
grating DPPs, it is possible to facilitate the tracking of materials and 
products throughout their lifecycle, from production to disposal.
